item.title: Morgans’ Stickley: S&P 500 up after every midterm since 1950 as Nvidia looks cheap
item.description:
A strong post-midterm seasonal record gives dip buyers a historical anchor, but the AI sell-off shows that policy risk to the data centre build-out is now a live variable for tech valuations. Nvidia’s results next week are the near-term test: guidance of more than $100 billion in revenue would back the view that fundamentals have decoupled from the share price. Stickley’s link between the election result and lower oil prices matters for the inflation outlook. If oil keeps easing, it could temper Fed hike expectations, which would support equities. For now that is his interpretation, not an established trend.

---

History says buy the post-midterm dip, and Morgans’ Stickley is doing so carefully, with Nvidia’s results next week the first real test.

Summary:

  • Morgans’ Jack Stickley told ausbiz that the S&P 500 has risen in the six and 12 months after every midterm election since 1950, by about 14% and 15%
  • He sees the Democratic sweep of Congress reining in parts of Trump’s agenda rather than derailing markets
  • He said the chip sell-off followed a very strong run and elevated valuations, but fundamentals remain strong
  • Nvidia has a large backlog, guidance of more than $100 billion in quarterly revenue and a forward P/E around 11 times, he said
  • He is adding to tech gradually ahead of Nvidia’s results next week, and favours building positions on pullbacks

The historical pattern of US stocks rallying after midterm elections remains intact despite Wall Street’s sharp technology sell-off, Jack Stickley of Australian stockbroker Morgans said in an interview with ausbiz.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has risen in both the six-month and 12-month periods following every US midterm election, Stickley said, with gains of about 14% and 15% respectively. He noted that a clean sweep of Congress by the party opposing the president has happened before, citing the Clinton era. In his view, the result mainly reins in parts of President Donald Trump’s policy agenda rather than changing the market’s direction. If the historical trend holds, he said, investors could be in for a good six to 12 months.

Stickley believes the election outcome has also reshaped the macro backdrop. He said voters had pushed back against the US data centre build-out and the war, and that Democratic control of both the Senate and the House creates an incentive to end the conflict, which he said had sent oil prices lower.

On technology, Stickley acknowledged the scale of the recent sell-off. He described a sudden one-day slide in which the semiconductor index fell about 12% and Nvidia around 9%, wiping roughly half a trillion dollars of market value. He said the sector had enjoyed an exceptionally strong run and that valuations had arguably become elevated. Even so, he believes the fundamentals remain strong, pointing to robust earnings growth.

Nvidia is his clearest example. Stickley said the chipmaker has clear visibility, a large order backlog and guidance for more than $100 billion in revenue next quarter, while its forward price-to-earnings ratio of around 11 times looks very cheap. He suggested setting aside the personal issues facing chief executive Jensen Huang and focusing on the business. He is not buying aggressively ahead of Nvidia’s results next week, he said, but he is starting to add exposure to the sector.

(Earlier: Mizuho’s Klein calls Nvidia ‘silly cheap’ below 10x earnings despite Huang uncertainty)

He cautioned that upcoming catalysts will test the AI investment case, particularly around the data centre rollout and the memory and chip suppliers at its core.

Closer to home, Stickley said Australian banks are holding up despite the cash rate rising to 4.85%, while consumer-facing companies are under pressure. His broader advice is to build positions gradually in high-quality names on pullbacks rather than trying to time the bottom.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Three drivers setting gold’s tone as December Fed hike bets build, according to Standard Chartered
item.description:
Gold’s drop on the CPI data shows how tightly the metal is now tied to Fed hike pricing, and therefore to oil. With a December quarter-point hike fully priced, any further rise in odds of a half-point move is likely to pressure bullion toward the support Standard Chartered has flagged, near $3,886. Equities are now a third driver: risk-off moves in stocks have not reliably supported gold during this conflict. The bank’s call for a softer dollar and steady central bank buying gives longer-term holders a reason to stay put, but the near-term path runs through December’s decision.

---

Fed speak is hawkish:

  • Fed’s Goolsbee calls CPI ‘borderline disturbing’, flags three inflation worries
  • Fed’s Paulson backs further gradual rate hikes, names three triggers for faster action
  • More from Fed’s Bowman: Shifts focus to inflation, wants AI and Middle East risks to ease first

---

Gold has kept its footing above $4,000, but with oil feeding Fed hike bets, Standard Chartered’s $4,700 target depends on a softer dollar arriving later rather than sooner.

Summary:

  • Standard Chartered said gold continues to trade above the key $4,000 level, with oil, inflation risks and equities setting the tone
  • Spot gold fell nearly 3% to around $4,020 on Tuesday after October CPI rose 0.4% month on month, against 0.3% expected
  • A December quarter-point Fed hike is fully priced, and half-point odds rose to around 10%
  • The bank stays overweight gold, with three-month and 12-month targets of $4,350 and $4,700
  • It expects Fed hikes in December and H1 2027 to a peak of 4.25% to 4.50%, and has flagged $3,886 as key support

Gold is still holding above the key $4,000 an ounce level despite a sharp sell-off after hotter-than-expected US inflation data, Standard Chartered said. Crude oil, inflation risks and equity markets are setting the tone, according to the bank, as traders focus on the Federal Reserve’s December meeting.

Spot gold fell nearly 3% on Tuesday to trade around $4,020 an ounce in the US session, while December futures dropped close to 2% to around $4,035. The metal had opened above $4,100 for the first time since October 22, but reversed after October consumer prices rose 0.4% on the month, above the 0.3% expected. The data lifted the dollar and Treasury yields, raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion.

Rate expectations shifted with the release. A quarter-point Fed hike in December is now fully priced, and the probability of a half-point move rose to around 10% from zero before the data, according to CME FedWatch. Fed Governor Christopher Waller had said earlier that a hot CPI reading could lead him to support a bigger increase.

Standard Chartered’s longer-term view remains constructive. In a report earlier this month, the bank said it remains overweight gold but trimmed its three-month target to $4,350 an ounce and its 12-month target to $4,700. It expects the Fed to raise rates in December and again in the first half of 2027, taking the target range to a peak of 4.25% to 4.50% before easing in the second half of next year. A softer dollar and continued buying by emerging-market central banks should drive gains over 12 months, it said, even though rising bond yields and a firmer dollar have been recent headwinds.

The bank has also flagged downside risk in the near term. In late October, it warned that gold needs to hold support around $3,886 after slipping below $4,000, or risk a deeper correction.

The pattern this year has been clear: rising oil prices from the Iran war have fed inflation and Fed hike expectations, and gold has struggled under that pressure rather than rallying as a haven. With December’s decision looming, oil and the next inflation data will decide whether the $4,000 floor holds. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SoftBank shares down after swings to $7 billion Q2 loss on $3.7 billion US data centre power hit
item.description:
The loss confirms that the cost of building AI infrastructure is now hitting the income statement, not just valuations, which adds to the wider debate about returns on AI spending. Record NAV and steady leverage limit balance-sheet concern. But the drop in pro forma NAV to around ¥44.7 trillion at November 9 prices shows how exposed SoftBank is to the recent tech sell-off. Any official OpenAI revaluation is the clearest potential positive catalyst for the shares. The data centre power writedown also adds to the evidence that power supply is a binding constraint on AI capacity growth, an issue also raised in UBS’s latest strategy note.

---

Posting ICYMI. SoftBank Group reported on Tuesday, November 10, after the Tokyo market close.

---

SoftBank paid up early for power to run AI data centres, and the bill has landed in its quarterly results, while the OpenAI upside is still waiting to be booked.

Summary:

  • SoftBank Group posted a fiscal Q2 net loss of about ¥1.12 trillion ($7 billion), against a ¥2.5 trillion profit a year earlier
  • A roughly $3.7 billion writedown on advance payments for US data centre power equipment was the largest hit, alongside Intel losses and higher financing costs
  • Revenue of ¥2.22 trillion beat the ¥2.02 trillion consensus
  • NAV reached a record ¥59.8 trillion at end-September, with LTV at 15.9%, but stood at about ¥44.7 trillion at November 9 prices
  • A further ¥3 trillion OpenAI investment lifted the stake to about 13%, and the new funding round valuation is not yet reflected

SoftBank Group swung to a net loss of about ¥1.12 trillion ($7 billion) in its fiscal second quarter, reversing a ¥2.5 trillion profit a year earlier, as a writedown on US AI data centre equipment, a fall in its Intel holding and higher financing costs weighed on results.

The biggest single hit was a roughly $3.7 billion (about ¥600 billion) writedown on nonrefundable advance payments for power-generation equipment intended for US data centres. A company executive said on the earnings call that SoftBank had made bridge investments early to secure the equipment in anticipation of shortages. Declines in investments including Intel and rising financing expenses added to the loss.

The top line was stronger. Revenue for the July to September quarter came in at ¥2.22 trillion, ahead of the LSEG consensus estimate of ¥2.02 trillion, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing.

For the first half of the fiscal year, SoftBank booked investment gains of about ¥1.7 trillion, down ¥2.2 trillion from a year earlier, leaving a net loss of around ¥770 billion for the six months.

The balance sheet tells a different story. Net asset value rose to a record ¥59.8 trillion at the end of September, up ¥20 trillion from the end of the last fiscal year. The loan-to-value ratio held at 15.9%, and the group kept about ¥5 trillion in liquidity. Recent market volatility has taken a toll, however: at November 9 prices, pro forma NAV stood at about ¥44.7 trillion.

OpenAI remains central to the investment case. SoftBank completed a further ¥3 trillion investment in the ChatGPT maker during the period, taking its stake to roughly 13%. It said any increase in OpenAI’s valuation from a new funding round has not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement, which leaves potential upside for future quarters.

SoftBank also said this week that it would commit, together with Grab and Malaysia’s PETROS, a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia.

The results highlight the cost of SoftBank’s aggressive push into AI infrastructure. Investors will be watching the OpenAI revaluation and the group’s financing costs as the main swing factors in the second half.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australian investor home lending plunges 32% in Q3 as tax curbs and RBA hikes bite harder
item.description:
A drop in home lending this sharp gives the RBA more evidence that its five hikes this year are biting. That supports the case for a pause after November’s split decision, and it is a modest headwind for the Australian dollar. Short-dated Australian government bond yields may be sensitive to any further sign that housing is cooling faster than the central bank expects. Bank stocks face slower mortgage growth, especially in investor lending, which has traditionally been a profitable segment. With energy-driven inflation still the RBA’s main worry, oil prices remain the swing factor for whether housing weakness is enough to keep rates on hold.

-

Tax changes, lending caps and five rate hikes have all hit Australian property investors at once, and the result is a collapse in landlord borrowing.

Summary:

  • Australian home loan values fell 15.5% q/q in Q3, against expectations of an 8% drop and a 5.2% fall in Q2
  • Investor lending plunged 32.3%, after falling 10.2% in Q2
  • Owner-occupier loan values fell 5.3%, after a 1.9% fall in Q2
  • The May budget ended negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night and curbed the capital gains tax discount
  • APRA has capped high debt-to-income lending since February, and the RBA has hiked five times this year to 4.85%

The value of new Australian home loans fell 15.5% in the September quarter, nearly twice the 8% decline economists had expected, as lending to property investors collapsed in the wake of government tax changes and a year of Reserve Bank of Australia rate hikes.

Investor lending was the main drag, plunging 32.3% on the quarter after a 10.2% fall in the June quarter. Owner-occupier loan values fell a more modest 5.3%, following a 1.9% decline previously. The overall drop was a sharp acceleration from the 5.2% fall recorded in the prior quarter.

The split between investors and owner-occupiers suggests policy is doing much of the work. In the May federal budget, the government moved to end negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night, keeping it only for newly built properties, and also announced curbs to the capital gains tax discount on established dwellings. Negative gearing lets investors offset rental losses against other income. The government argued the housing market needed rebalancing, with most investor credit going towards existing homes rather than new supply. The major banks moved quickly to reflect the changes in how they assess investor loan applications, reducing borrowing capacity for many landlords.

Those measures came on top of tighter lending rules. From February, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority required banks to limit new loans at six or more times a borrower’s income to 20% of new mortgage lending, measured separately for owner-occupiers and investors.

Monetary policy has added further pressure. The RBA has raised its cash rate five times this year, in February, March, May, September and November, taking it to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, as it fights inflation that has been pushed higher by energy costs. The November decision was split 6-3, and the statement dropped earlier language about further increases.

The RBA’s own November Statement on Monetary Policy had already flagged a steep fall in investor lending, describing the drop in investor loan commitments as the largest in any hiking cycle on record. Governor Michele Bullock said a pullback in investor demand was normal in a housing downturn. The bigger fall compared with owner-occupiers, though, suggests the budget changes are having an effect.

The figures strengthen the case that housing is cooling quickly, which may feed into the RBA’s assessment of whether its tightening has gone far enough.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6855 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NIESR sees UK inflation above BoE target for four years, peaking at 4.4% in 2027
item.description:
A longer inflation overshoot driven by the Iran war’s energy shock keeps oil prices at the centre of the UK rate outlook: every sustained rise in crude raises the risk of further second-round effects on wages. NIESR’s call for only one more hike contrasts with market pricing of two or three. Its view that rates may need to reach around 5% points the other way, and supports the case for gilt yields and sterling to stay sensitive to energy-led data surprises. The critique of the October budget adds fiscal credibility risk on top, which could weigh on longer-dated gilts if borrowing plans keep slipping.

---

The Bank of England not the only one in deep doggy-doo:

  • Fed’s Goolsbee calls CPI ‘borderline disturbing’, flags three inflation worries

--- NIESR sees a longer inflation overshoot in Britain, and a BoE that may be doing less than the job requires.

Summary:

  • NIESR forecasts UK inflation will peak at 4.4% in February 2027, up from a 3.8% peak in its July forecast
  • It sees inflation above the BoE’s 2% target in 2027, 2028 and 2029, returning to target in late 2030
  • It expects one more BoE hike, in February, while markets price two or three by end-2027, and says rates may need to reach around 5%
  • The 2026 growth forecast is raised to 1.6% from 1.1%, slowing to 1.1% in 2027 and 0.9% in 2028
  • Unemployment is seen rising to a peak of 5.1% in 2031, with wage growth averaging 3.9% over three years
  • NIESR said the October budget did little to strengthen the public finances

UK inflation will stay above the Bank of England’s 2% target for the next four years as the Iran war’s energy shock feeds through into wages, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) forecast on Tuesday. The think-tank also raised its outlook for growth.

It now expects inflation to peak at 4.4% in February 2027, up from the 3.8% peak it forecast in July. It sees inflation remaining above target through 2027, 2028 and 2029 before returning to 2% in late 2030, a year later than it previously expected. Second-round effects on wages are the main reason for the delay.

The outlook for policy is where NIESR parts company with markets. Investors are pricing two or three quarter-point rate hikes by the end of next year, but the think-tank expects the BoE to raise rates only once more, in February. NIESR also said rates would need to rise to around 5% to bring inflation back to target over the medium term, which suggests it thinks a single hike would not be enough to meet the goal on time. The BoE raised Bank Rate to 4% from 3.75% last week, its first increase in more than three years.

NIESR Director David Aikman said the economy had held up better than expected this year but now faces the twin pressures of higher energy prices and rising global borrowing costs. He said the policy response on both the monetary and fiscal sides is a domestic choice, and that decisions on both fronts are being put off.

On the fiscal side, NIESR said finance minister John Healey’s October budget did little to strengthen the public finances. Difficult decisions on tax and spending had largely been deferred, it said, and plans to reduce borrowing lacked credibility.

Growth has been more resilient than expected. NIESR raised its 2026 forecast to 1.6% from 1.1%, citing stronger government spending and business investment, partly driven by AI. It expects growth to slow to 1.1% in 2027 and 0.9% in 2028. Unemployment is projected to edge up from 4.8% in 2026 to a peak of 5.1% in 2031, with wage growth averaging 3.9% over the next three years.

The gap between NIESR’s single-hike forecast and market pricing will be tested at the BoE’s next meetings, with energy prices and wage settlements the key data to watch. 

---

NIESR is Britain’s longest-established independent economic research institute. It was founded in 1938 and is based in London. It is a non-profit charity, independent of government and political parties, and it publishes regular forecasts for the UK and global economies, which are widely watched alongside those from the Bank of England and the government’s fiscal watchdog. Its director, David Aikman, joined in 2023 from the Bank of England, where he worked on financial stability.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Goolsbee calls CPI ‘borderline disturbing’, flags three inflation worries
item.description:
Strong language like this from Goolsbee adds weight to the hawkish run of Fed commentary after the CPI report, and it strengthens pricing for a December hike. His focus on services and expectations points to concern about entrenched inflation, not transitory shocks, which raises the risk of a longer hiking cycle. That backdrop supports the US dollar and front-end Treasury yields, and remains a headwind for gold. With energy feeding the cost side of inflation, oil prices stay central to how hawkish the Fed may need to be.

---

Earlier:

  • Fed’s Paulson backs further gradual rate hikes, names three triggers for faster action
  • Fed's Bowman: Persistent inflation, firming labor conditions suggest 'work to do'

---

Goolsbee has gone from cautious to alarmed: sticky services prices and broad overheating make inflation a problem the Fed now has to confront.

Summary:

  • Goolsbee told PBS NewsHour that the October CPI report was borderline disturbing and that the US has a real inflation issue
  • He said the most troubling element is that services inflation is not coming down
  • He described inflation as driven by both cost and demand, and fears broad overheating across many prices
  • He said it would be a major concern if inflation gets built into expectations
  • The job market is steady and stable, he said, and everything is on the table to get inflation back to target

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said Tuesday’s consumer price report was “borderline disturbing”, warning in an interview with PBS NewsHour that the US has a real inflation problem that policymakers will have to address.

Goolsbee said the most troubling element of the October data was that services inflation is not coming down. Services prices tend to reflect domestic demand and wage costs more than goods prices do. A lack of progress there suggests price pressures are becoming more entrenched rather than fading as one-off shocks unwind.

He described inflation as being driven from both the cost side and the demand side. His fear, he said, is the emergence of overheating across a broad range of prices, rather than increases confined to a few categories. At the same time, he noted that the job market remains steady and stable, which removes one of the usual arguments for holding back on tighter policy.

Goolsbee said a key concern would be inflation becoming built into expectations, and that the Fed would have to come to terms with it if price pressures stay persistent. He also pointed out that business investment is affected by interest rates, suggesting he is weighing how higher borrowing costs could feed through to spending. He stressed that everything is always on the table and that the Fed must bring inflation down to its target.

The interview added to a run of hawkish commentary from Fed officials after October’s CPI showed a larger-than-expected increase. Earlier on Tuesday, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said further gradual rate hikes seem appropriate, while Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said she was shifting her focus to inflation. Markets are pricing strong odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting.

Goolsbee’s choice of language stands out for an official who has often struck a more measured tone. With services inflation sticky and the labour market holding up, December’s decision will show how far policymakers are prepared to go to stop inflation becoming entrenched.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Paulson backs further gradual rate hikes, names three triggers for faster action
item.description:
Paulson’s comments add a voting member’s voice to the hawkish chorus after the hot CPI report, which reinforces pricing for a December hike and a follow-up in January. Her emphasis on gradual steps tempers the case for a half-point move, but her three triggers for faster action leave that door open if data keeps running hot. That combination supports the US dollar and front-end Treasury yields, while a firmer hiking path remains a headwind for gold. Because she names energy prices as an inflation driver, any further Middle East-driven gains in oil now feed directly into the Fed’s tightening calculus.

---

Earlier:

  • More from Fed’s Bowman: Shifts focus to inflation, wants AI and Middle East risks to ease first

---

Paulson favours steady hikes rather than sprints, but has set out exactly what would make her pick up the pace.

Summary:

  • Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, a 2026 FOMC voter, said further gradual tightening seems appropriate
  • She said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to return inflation to 2%, with underlying inflation stuck between 2.5% and 3%
  • She would favour moving faster if inflation expectations drift up, wage pressures build or underlying inflation rises
  • Paulson said the October CPI rise of 0.4% shows inflation pressures persist, driven by tariffs, energy and AI investment
  • Futures price strong odds of a quarter-point hike on December 8-9 from the current 3.75% to 4% range, and another in January

Philadelphia Federal Reserve President Anna Paulson said on Tuesday that further gradual interest rate increases appear appropriate to bring down elevated inflation, and that she would favour moving faster if price pressures worsen.

In the text of a speech prepared for a gathering in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania, Paulson said monetary policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to return inflation to the Fed’s 2% target. Inflation has run above that goal for more than five years, she noted, with underlying pressures holding between 2.5% and 3%. She said the exact path of rates will depend on how conditions evolve and that she will be watching the data closely.

Paulson, a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee this year, argued that a gradual approach has served the Fed well. In her view, it gives the economy time to adjust to higher borrowing costs while allowing policymakers room to assess the effects of their decisions. She said she has supported the Fed’s recent rate decisions and described bringing inflation down as her main priority, with the economy proving stronger than expected and the job market robust and stable.

She also set out the conditions under which she would favour a quicker pace. Paulson said she would want to act more quickly if inflation expectations drift higher, if wage pressures build, or if underlying inflation rises. She described risks to the inflation outlook as high and said the effects of AI and energy on prices are hard to gauge.

Her remarks came after October consumer price data showed a larger-than-expected rise, with the overall index up 0.4% on the month. Paulson said the report suggests inflation pressures remain very much present, pointing to tariffs, energy prices and AI investment as drivers. Economists saw signs that price increases once concentrated in a few areas are spreading more broadly.

Futures markets are pricing strong odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting, from the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, and a further increase in late January. Before the CPI release, Governor Christopher Waller said a reading like October’s could lead him to support a half-point move. The December meeting is now the key test of whether the Fed sticks with gradual steps or speeds up. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Mizuho’s Klein calls Nvidia ‘silly cheap’ below 10x earnings despite Huang uncertainty
item.description:
The valuation case gives dip buyers a clear anchor: a forward multiple below 10 times for a market leader with fast-growing earnings is rare. The open-ended board review limits how far that argument can work in the near term, because markets tend to price timeline uncertainty harshly. As Nvidia carries so much weight in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, headlines about the review are likely to keep moving the indexes, not just the stock. The observation that tech now trades below the broader market could support rotation back into the sector once the leadership question is clearer.

---

Nvidia’s valuation now looks more like a company in decline than one at the centre of AI, and analysts say that mismatch is the opportunity, provided the leadership question resolves.

Summary:

  • Mizuho’s Jordan Klein told CNBC that Nvidia’s forward P/E below 10 times signals extreme undervaluation
  • Klein said the stock is pricing in post-election concerns and uncertainty over CEO Jensen Huang’s leadership
  • He called losing Huang a significant risk and said investors see him as irreplaceable, with the open-ended timeline the biggest concern
  • Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation, and the shares fell about 4% on Monday
  • Another strategist called the weakness a potential rare opportunity and noted that tech trades cheaper than the S&P 500 for the first time in over a decade

Nvidia shares may be “silly cheap” after a sharp derating, offering a compelling buying opportunity despite uncertainty over chief executive Jensen Huang, Mizuho Securities technology analyst Jordan Klein told CNBC.

Klein pointed to the chipmaker’s forward price-to-earnings multiple, which has fallen below 10 times, as a sign of extreme undervaluation. Multiples that low, he said, are normally seen at companies with structural problems or businesses in long-term decline, and Nvidia is neither. In his view, the stock has been derating for some time, with earnings growing much faster than the share price. It is now pricing in substantial uncertainty linked to post-election concerns and to questions over Huang’s leadership.

Those questions follow the board’s decision to open an independent investigation after reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia has said Huang fully supports the review and will cooperate with it. The shares fell about 4% on Monday as investors weighed the leadership risk.

Klein acknowledged that losing Huang would be a significant risk. He described the chief executive as a visionary for Nvidia and for the wider technology and AI industries, and said investors regard him as irreplaceable. Nvidia has a deep bench of talent, Klein said, but the open-ended timeline of the situation is the market’s biggest concern.

Another strategist took a more upbeat view. His firm recently added Nvidia to its list of AI stocks to buy for next year, and he suggested the current weakness could prove a rare opportunity if leadership remains sound. He also noted that technology stocks as a group are trading at a lower valuation than the S&P 500 for the first time in more than a decade.

He described Nvidia as one of the central companies in the AI revolution, if not the central one. Even so, the strategist said he was confident the broader AI transformation would not be seriously derailed even if turbulence at the chipmaker continues.

The outcome and timing of the board’s review are now the key variables for the stock, along with whether the valuation discount Klein highlights begins to attract buyers.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic reserves up to 20% of its $64 billion IPO for retail investors
item.description:
A retail tranche this large widens the buyer base for a very large deal, which may help support demand at the top of the $70 to $78 range. The trade-off is pricing discipline: if retail buyers are less price-sensitive than institutions, the final price could be pushed higher, which leaves less room for gains after listing. Together with SpaceX’s matching 20% allocation, the move suggests mega-cap listings are increasingly turning to individual investors to absorb supply. How the deal is received will also be read as a gauge of investor appetite for AI exposure more broadly, including listed names such as CoreWeave.

--- Anthropic is offering a fifth of its IPO to individual investors, which widens access to the deal, but analysts warn the structure may favour the company more than the buyers.

Summary:

  • Anthropic expects to allocate up to 20% of its IPO’s Class A shares to retail investors in the US and other countries, depending on demand
  • It is offering 801.4 million shares at $70 to $78 each, and existing investors are selling 23.6 million more, for a total of up to about $64 billion
  • Underwriters have a 30-day option on up to 123.75 million additional shares
  • The allocation compares with about 10% at Arm, about 8% at Reddit and up to 5% at Instacart, while SpaceX has also set aside 20%
  • Analysts link the decision to the deal’s size and the brand benefit, but warn that retail buyers may be less price-sensitive than institutions

Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, expects to allocate up to 20% of the Class A shares in its initial public offering to retail investors. That is an unusually large share, and it could give individuals wider access to one of the year’s biggest listings.

In its filing, the company said retail investors in the United States and other countries could receive up to that proportion of the shares on offer, with the final split depending on demand. Anthropic is offering 801.4 million Class A shares at a price range of $70 to $78 each, while existing investors are selling a further 23.6 million shares. At the top of the range, the offering would raise up to about $64 billion. Underwriters also have a 30-day option to buy up to 123.75 million additional shares at the IPO price, less underwriting discounts and commissions.

The retail allocation is well above recent precedents in large technology listings. Arm Holdings set aside about 10% of its shares for retail investors in 2023, Reddit reserved about 8% for eligible users and moderators, and Instacart offered up to 5%. CoreWeave did not have a dedicated retail tranche, and retail investors were not given direct allocations in SK Hynix’s US depositary receipt offering. SpaceX has taken the same approach as Anthropic, with a 20% retail allocation.

Analysts said the decision largely reflects the scale of the deal. One analyst said that at a potential valuation of $1.4 trillion to $2 trillion, the volume of stock to be placed is large even for major institutions. Tapping retail demand also benefits the brand, the analyst said, given how many individuals use Claude. The same analyst cautioned that retail buyers can be less sensitive to price than institutions, calling the structure “a great deal for the company, but not necessarily for the people buying.” Retail demand is also expected to exceed the shares available to individual investors.

The underwriting syndicate includes Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Barclays, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, Deutsche Bank, RBC Capital Markets and UBS.

Final pricing, and how much of the retail tranche is taken up, will show how far individual investors’ enthusiasm for AI extends to paying up at listing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Reuters Tankan: Japan manufacturer mood hits +27, highest in over five years on chips
item.description:
The broad-based jump in confidence, especially among service firms, adds to the picture of a Japanese economy strong enough to cope with higher interest rates. Combined with the reported tight labour market and persistent cost pressure, that could support expectations of further Bank of Japan tightening, which would be supportive for the yen. For equities, the strength in electronics and precision machinery reinforces the chip-led earnings story behind Japan’s tech and equipment names. The caution on passing costs on to customers is a reminder that margin pressure has not gone away.

---

Japan Inc’s mood is at multi-year highs on chips and services, even as rising prices and borrowing costs start to pinch.

Summary:

  • Reuters Tankan manufacturers’ index rose to +27 in November from +22, the highest since August 2021
  • Non-manufacturers’ index surged to +35 from +23, the highest since June 2018
  • Electronics jumped to +39 from +25 on strong memory chip demand, and precision machinery rose to +42 from +38
  • Services and others more than doubled to +43 from +19, with firms citing a tight labour market
  • Rising prices and higher interest rates weighed on both sectors
  • Outlook for February: manufacturers +28, non-manufacturers +29

Japanese manufacturers’ confidence climbed to its highest level in more than five years in November, lifted by booming semiconductor demand, while sentiment among non-manufacturers reached its strongest in over eight years, according to the Reuters Tankan poll.

The manufacturers’ index rose to +27 from +22 in October, its highest reading since August 2021. The non-manufacturers’ index surged to +35 from +23, a level last seen in June 2018. The monthly poll is closely watched as a leading indicator for the Bank of Japan’s quarterly Tankan business survey. It was conducted from October 27 to November 6, and 214 of the 508 firms surveyed responded. Readings are calculated by subtracting the percentage of pessimistic responses from optimistic ones, so a positive figure signals net optimism.

Chipmakers and their suppliers drove the gain among manufacturers. Sentiment in electronics jumped to +39 from +25, with one respondent describing demand for semiconductors, particularly memory chips, as very strong. Precision machinery, which includes some chip equipment makers, improved to +42 from +38 on robust domestic and overseas orders. Another machinery firm said shipments to the semiconductor market had reached unprecedented levels. Oil refining and ceramics rose to +25 from +14, while chemicals improved to +33 from +27.

The service side of the economy was just as upbeat. Information and communications sentiment rose to +29 from +8 on strong orders, while services and others more than doubled to +43 from +19. One manager pointed to persistently tight labour market conditions keeping demand for staff high.

Not everything was positive. Firms in both sectors said rising prices and higher interest rates were weighing on business, and some reported difficulty passing increased costs on to customers.

Looking ahead, manufacturers expect sentiment to edge up to +28 in February, while non-manufacturers see confidence easing to +29, still well above recent levels. For the Bank of Japan, the combination of strong business confidence, a tight labour market and cost pressures will be one input as it weighs the outlook for policy. Its own quarterly Tankan will be the next major read on corporate sentiment.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

UBS’s preference for semiconductors, hyperscalers and the Nasdaq 100 over the Russell 2000 points to a continued tilt toward large-cap AI beneficiaries rather than a broad rotation. The near-term warning on positioning and technical factors suggests volatility is likely to persist into year-end. Rising oil prices are named as one of the drags on valuations, which ties the equity outlook partly to how energy markets develop. Data center construction policy after the midterms is the new variable to watch for the AI capex trade.

---

UBS says the S&P 500 has already been marked down for its worries, and with earnings still growing, history favours the bulls.

Summary:

  • UBS kept its year-end 2027 S&P 500 target at 8,900 and set an end-2028 target of 9,600
  • It forecasts EPS rising 18% to $430 in 2027 and 14% to $490 in 2028, with 8,900 equal to about 18 times 2028 earnings
  • The forward P/E has fallen about 20% this year despite earnings growth of around a third, and historically the index has returned a median 20% after a P/E drop of more than 10%
  • UBS warned that the near term remains volatile and driven by positioning, but sees scope for a rebound early next year
  • Data center construction pauses after the midterms put about 30% of planned 2028 US capacity additions at risk
  • UBS favours semiconductors, software, hyperscalers, health care and financials, and prefers the Nasdaq 100 over the Russell 2000

UBS has kept its year-end 2027 target for the S&P 500 at 8,900, arguing that this year’s sharp fall in valuations has historically set the stage for strong returns, according to a note from US equity strategist Keith Parker reported by Investing.com.

The target is built on earnings. UBS forecasts S&P 500 earnings per share will grow 18% to $430 in 2027 and a further 14% to $490 in 2028, and the 8,900 level equates to about 18 times that 2028 figure. The bank also set an end-2028 target of 9,600. Seeking Alpha reported that UBS lowered its end-2026 target to 7,900, which would leave the 2027 call about 13% higher.

Parker’s central argument is that valuations have already absorbed a lot of bad news. The index’s forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen about 20% this year, even though earnings are on track to grow by around a third. He attributed the derating to worries about returns on AI spending and its regulation, higher bond yields and credit spreads, rising oil prices and weaker share buybacks. History offers support, he said: in years following a fall of more than 10% in the index’s P/E ratio, the S&P 500 has delivered a median return of 20%.

UBS was cautious about the near term. It described the market as highly volatile and increasingly driven by positioning and technical factors, which makes its near-term target harder to reach. Even so, it sees a growing chance of a rebound early next year once the derating and de-risking have run their course. It also expects further evidence of accelerating AI adoption through the first half of 2027.

The main risk the bank flagged is further out. State-level pauses on data center construction following the midterm elections put about 30% of planned US capacity additions in 2028 at risk, which UBS said skews 2028 risks lower. It plans to revisit its forecasts as policy details emerge, likely next year.

On positioning, UBS prefers semiconductors to tech hardware and is overweight software, hyperscalers, health care and financials. It favours the Nasdaq 100 over the Russell 2000, along with companies that have strong balance sheets. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Carney says Canada has made no decision on lifting its Arctic offshore drilling ban
item.description:
There is no near-term supply effect. Arctic offshore projects would take many years to develop even if the ban were lifted, so this is a long-dated policy story, not a price driver. The value for traders is in the direction of travel: Ottawa is openly trying to expand energy output to offset US tariff pressure, and the 2028 expiry is now a clear decision point. Any eventual move to open the Arctic would add to the longer-term North American supply outlook, but for now the official line is that nothing has changed.

---

Carney says Canada’s Arctic drilling ban is not up for grabs yet, but with a 2028 expiry and an energy-first growth agenda, the question will not go away.

Summary:

  • Carney said his government has not decided whether to lift Canada’s Arctic offshore oil and gas moratorium
  • A Toronto Star report had said Ottawa was considering lifting the ban
  • A budget line of C$11 million (about US$8 million) over four years for Arctic offshore oversight is capacity funding for Inuit leadership, Carney said
  • The moratorium dates from 2016, is reviewed every five years and expires in 2028
  • Carney is seeking to grow Canada’s energy sector to support the economy against US tariffs

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that his government has not decided whether to lift its moratorium on offshore oil and gas exploration in the Arctic, Reuters reported. His comments push back against suggestions that Ottawa is preparing to open the region to drilling.

They followed a Toronto Star report on Monday, citing a Department of Finance official, that the government was considering lifting the ban. Attention had also been drawn to a line in last week’s federal budget allocating C$11 million (about US$8 million) over four years to support governance and oversight of offshore oil and gas activity in the Arctic Ocean.

Speaking to reporters in Montreal, Carney described that funding as capacity support for Inuit leadership, which jointly manages natural resources in the North with the federal government. He said it was “absolutely not” a decision about the moratorium.

The ban has been in place since 2016, when Canada and the United States agreed to restrict Arctic offshore exploration to protect the region’s marine ecosystem from the risk of oil spills. Washington later reopened parts of its Arctic to drilling under President Donald Trump, but Canada’s moratorium stayed in place. The policy is reviewed every five years and is due to expire in 2028.

That expiry date keeps the issue alive. Canada’s Arctic holds significant undeveloped oil and gas reserves, and some Northern leaders, including Nunavut’s premier, have called for the region to be opened up to support economic self-sufficiency. Carney has also been seeking to expand Canada’s energy sector to bolster the economy in the face of US tariffs. In pursuit of growth he has eased a number of climate regulations, drawing criticism from environmental groups.

For now, the government’s message is that nothing has changed. The next marker is the moratorium’s 2028 review. Any shift in policy would have to fit with both Ottawa’s push to grow energy output and its commitments to Inuit and territorial self-government.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Private oil inventory survey shows huge headline build vs. draw expected
item.description:
This week the API data carries extra weight, because the delayed EIA release gives traders longer to position on the industry figures. Middle East supply disruption is keeping crude highly sensitive to any sign of tightening or loosening in US balances, so early inventory signals have a bigger effect on prices than usual. Product stocks matter as well, since gasoline and distillate moves feed into views on refinery margins and winter fuel demand. The main risk sits with Thursday’s EIA report, which could quickly reverse any move made on the API numbers if the two diverge sharply.

---

  • The expected I had for the headline was a 1mn barrel draw. 

---

The API has the first word on US oil stocks, and this week, with the EIA delayed by the holiday, it keeps that role a day longer than usual.

Summary:

  • The API has released its weekly US oil inventory survey for the week ended November 6
  • The API is an industry trade group that compiles voluntary data from oil companies, and it is released on Tuesday afternoons, US time
  • The EIA, part of the US Department of Energy, uses mandatory surveys and is the market benchmark
  • The EIA report adds production, trade, refinery runs, implied demand and Strategic Petroleum Reserve data
  • The two reports can diverge, sometimes sharply, and the EIA figure usually takes over as the reference point
  • This week’s EIA report is delayed to Thursday at 12:00 ET (17:00 GMT) because of the Veterans Day holiday

The American Petroleum Institute (API) has released its weekly survey of US oil inventories, giving traders a first look at stock changes for the week ended November 6. The official figures from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) follow on Thursday, a day later than usual because of the Veterans Day holiday.

The two reports cover the same week and many of the same categories, including commercial crude stocks, inventories at the Cushing, Oklahoma, storage hub, and gasoline and distillate stocks. They differ in three key ways: who compiles them, how complete the data is, and when they are published.

The API is an industry trade association, and its weekly survey relies on figures that oil companies, refiners, pipeline operators and terminal owners submit voluntarily. The data goes first to subscribers on Tuesday afternoon, US time, and the headline numbers then circulate quickly through the market.

The EIA is the independent statistical agency of the US Department of Energy. Its Weekly Petroleum Status Report is built from mandatory surveys of companies across the supply chain, which gives it wider coverage. It is normally published at 10:30 a.m. Eastern time on Wednesdays. This week, the EIA’s schedule moves the release to Thursday at 12:00 p.m. Eastern (17:00 GMT).

The EIA report is also more detailed. As well as inventories, it includes domestic crude production, imports and exports, refinery runs and utilisation, implied demand for fuels, and holdings in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. That breadth is why traders treat it as the benchmark and the API figures as an early indication.

Because the two surveys use different methods and samples, their numbers can diverge, sometimes by several million barrels, and occasionally point in opposite directions. When the API and EIA agree, the API reading has usually set the tone in advance. When they differ, the EIA figure usually becomes the market’s reference point.

With Middle East supply disruption keeping oil markets sensitive to any shift in US balances, the extra day’s wait leaves the API reading as traders’ main inventory signal for longer than usual. Thursday’s EIA report will show whether it holds.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More from Fed’s Bowman: Shifts focus to inflation, wants AI and Middle East risks to ease first
item.description:
Overall the comments lean hawkish. Bowman’s shift in focus to inflation and her link to Middle East risk keep energy prices at the centre of the Fed debate, which supports the US dollar and front-end Treasury yields. Her emphasis on pace and timeline suggests a preference for gradual tightening rather than aggressive moves, which may temper any repricing toward bigger or faster hikes. For gold, a firmer case for further tightening has been a headwind during this conflict, not a support. Oil traders may read her remarks as a reminder that any further Middle East escalation now feeds directly into Fed policy risk.

---

Earlier:

  • Fed's Bowman: Persistent inflation, firming labor conditions suggest 'work to do'

---

Bowman has turned firmly toward the inflation fight, but her talk of pace and timeline suggests she would rather take it step by step than rush.

Summary:

  • Bowman said she is shifting her focus to inflation and that its lack of a downward trend should give the Fed pause
  • She would need to see AI and Middle East risks fade before she could be confident inflation will fall next year
  • Longer-term inflation expectations are very well anchored, she said, but they do not necessarily drive her thinking
  • She said the Fed needs to consider the pace and timeline of its response, citing last year’s gradual cuts, pause and resumption as a model
  • She does not expect AI to cost the US economy jobs overall, and sees productivity gains and new roles instead
  • On supervision, she expects to finalise the GSIB surcharge and Basel III rules in the coming weeks, with her focus moving to smaller-bank rules

Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said she is shifting her focus to inflation, arguing that the lack of a downward trend in price pressures should give policymakers pause. She added that she would need to see risks tied to artificial intelligence and the Middle East fade before she could be confident inflation will come down next year.

The remarks, made in a question-and-answer session on Tuesday, followed earlier comments in which Bowman said persistent inflation and firming labour market conditions suggest the Fed still has work to do. In those remarks, she estimated that core PCE inflation likely ran at 3.3% in October, driven by energy prices and AI-related demand.

Her latest comments were more mixed in tone. On one side, Bowman said longer-term inflation expectations remain very well anchored. She called expectations an important data point but said they do not necessarily drive her thinking, which suggests anchored expectations alone will not settle her policy view.

On the other side, she said the Fed needs to think about the pace and timeline for addressing inflation. She drew a parallel with the central bank’s approach last year, when it cut rates gradually, paused, and then resumed. In her view, a similarly measured, step-by-step approach could be used to tackle inflation in the coming months. That framing points to a preference for gradual tightening over a rapid move, rather than signalling any specific decision.

On the labour market, Bowman said she does not expect AI to rob the US economy of jobs. She expects the technology to make workers more productive, create new roles and remove less necessary ones.

Bowman also covered her supervisory brief. She said she hopes and expects to finalise rules on the surcharge for global systemically important banks (GSIBs) and on Basel III capital standards in the coming weeks, and that her attention has turned to rules and supervisory approaches for smaller banks. She noted that the Fed carries out ongoing cybersecurity examinations of banks and has seen a strong focus on finding and patching vulnerabilities. She also said open lines of communication with the Treasury are critically important.

Taken together, the comments keep the inflation fight at the centre of Bowman’s thinking, while her emphasis on pace suggests she favours a measured path. Upcoming inflation data, and any easing in energy and AI-related price pressures, will be key to how far that view moves.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

October CPI was the story. Headline inflation slowed from September, but both headline and core prices rose more than expected. The core reading mattered most. Before the release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller had flagged a 0.3% reading as the point where a larger December hike could come into play. That’s what the report showed at published precision, and traders raised the odds of a half-point move. images.investinglive.com.  The current numbers put a 50 bp hike in December at 10% while a 25 bp hike is the other 90%.  

The 2-year yield led the move higher, the dollar gained against every major currency in the late-session snapshot, and gold and silver fell. Anthropic’s IPO terms gave tech stocks an early lift, but the Nasdaq Composite ended the session snapshot down 0.74%. investinglive.com

The dollar rises across the board

The dollar gained the most against the Australian dollar, with AUDUSD down 0.91% to 0.6863, followed by a 0.75% decline in GBPUSD to 1.3339. EURUSD fell 0.55% to 1.1161, while USDJPY rose 0.55% to 158.77 (see technical post here). The dollar’s smallest gain was against the Canadian dollar, with USDCAD up 0.51% to 1.4189.

Treasury yields jump, led by the 2-year

  • 5-year yield 4.8121%, +15.31 basis points
  • 10-year yield 4.9875%, +12.55 basis points

The 10-year traded above 5% during the session and was back just below it in the late snapshot. The bigger move in the 2-year tells the story. Traders were repricing what the Fed might do over the next few meetings. A soft $42 billion 10-year auction added to the pressure. It stopped at 5.02%, 1 basis point above the when-issued yield, and the 2.46x bid-to-cover ratio fell short of the 2.60x average. US stocks give back the Anthropic bounce

  • S&P 500 7,520.93, −0.38%
  • Nasdaq Composite 20,065.87, −0.74%

Anthropic’s IPO gives tech a lift that fades

Anthropic kicked off its IPO roadshow with updated terms after retracting preliminary figures sent to bankers. The Claude maker and selling shareholders are offering 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each, for a deal worth up to $64.4 billion and an implied valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. Reports that orders covered the available shares helped push the Nasdaq indices into positive territory earlier in the session. The bounce faded. Demand for the offering is one barometer of investors’ appetite for AI, while today’s jump in yields raised the hurdle for growth-stock valuations across the market. investinglive.com

European stocks mostly higher, led by Spain

  • Spain’s IBEX 35 +0.98%
  • Italy’s FTSE MIB +0.69%
  • France’s CAC 40 +0.55%
  • Germany’s DAX +0.31%
  • UK’s FTSE 100 −0.29%. investinglive.com

US CPI. Headline slows, but core stays sticky

Headline CPI rose 0.4% in October versus 0.3% expected and 0.6% in September. Core CPI rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected, the third straight month at 0.3% on a rounded basis. The BLS had no October 2025 comparison because of last year’s government shutdown, so the October report came without year-over-year readings. September’s annual rates were 3.7% for headline and 2.6% for core.

Energy rose 0.7% after September’s 5.2% jump, helping explain the slowdown in headline CPI. Shelter rose 0.3% and accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase. Food rose 0.5%. Under the surface, motor vehicle insurance rose 0.7% and airfares climbed 0.4%, while used-car prices fell 1.2%. InvestingLive put core services excluding shelter, often called supercore, at roughly 0.4% for the month.

The distinction for the Fed is that the energy impulse cooled sharply while core inflation held its pace. The unrounded core reading was 0.297%, close enough to Waller’s 0.3% marker to get the market’s attention. October PCE and November payrolls are still due before the December meeting. PCE is the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, and payrolls will help show how much room the Fed has to tighten. images.investinglive.com

The Fed speakers, one by one

A number of Fed speakers did talk today and they were more hawkish him

Christopher Waller. Speaking before CPI, Waller said he would support a 25-basis-point December hike even if October inflation improved. He opened the door to a 50-basis-point move if core CPI came in at 0.3% or higher. He sees the labor market as broadly balanced and is concerned about how widely price increases have spread, including whether higher energy costs are feeding into other goods and services.

Michelle Bowman. Speaking after the release, Bowman said the CPI report suggested inflation pressures could persist longer and that labor-market conditions appeared to be firming. She pointed to October PCE and November payrolls as two inputs still to come before the December decision. She also wants to assess how durable AI-related demand is and how geopolitical risks feed through to the economy.

Jeff Schmid. The Kansas City Fed president called current policy fairly accommodative. Housing stood out as an area where rates may be biting, but he saw little evidence of restraint elsewhere. He also flagged concerning price trends beneath the energy headlines. His argument was that the current rate setting is doing too little to slow inflation. images.investinglive.com

Lorie Logan. The Dallas Fed president said she sees a need for at least two more quarter-point hikes and that the Fed may be able to move faster this winter. After those two moves, she would see a case for pausing to assess the economy. She also said higher bond yields signal that monetary policy still has work to do.

The overall message. All four put inflation front and center, but they emphasized different parts of the decision. Waller put the size of the December move in play. Logan laid out a path of at least two more increases. Schmid questioned whether current policy is restrictive enough, and Bowman emphasized the data still to come. The jump in the 2-year yield was the clearest sign that traders took the prospect of faster tightening seriously.

Oil slips. Metals and crypto fall harder.

WTI was down 0.56% at $86.36 after trading as low as $83.88, while Brent slipped 0.67% to $91.95. Hopes for progress in US–Iran talks remained in the background. Today’s softer crude prices offered some relief on energy costs, but the bond market took its cue from the CPI surprise and the Fed’s response. investinglive.com

Gold fell 2.59% to around $4,032 and silver dropped 3.54% to $51.52. A stronger dollar and higher Treasury yields were headwinds for both. Bitcoin fell 1.42% to around $73,881, moving in the same direction as growth stocks, while Ethereum lost 3.18% to $2,059.42.

The 2-year yield is the barometer going forward. October CPI brought a larger December hike into the conversation. The next test is whether October PCE confirms the persistence in core prices and whether November payrolls give the Fed room to move faster. investing.com

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Costco declares $30 special dividend worth $13.3 billion, renews $4 billion buyback
item.description:
A $30 payout goes well past the roughly $24 per share that analysts had estimated would match the yield of the 2024 special dividend, so it is likely to be read as a positive surprise on size, not just timing. In the past, Costco shares have firmed in the days after a special dividend is announced, as investors buy in to qualify before the record date. The bigger question for valuation is balance-sheet strength: returning $13.3 billion in one go uses a large share of the cash the company has built up. Over time, the renewed buyback also gives Costco more room to support the share count.

---

Earlier:

  • CoreWeave Q3 beats on seven key metrics, lifts full-year revenue and run-rate guidance

---

Costco has delivered the special dividend shareholders were waiting for, and at $30 a share it is twice the size of the last one.

Summary:

  • Costco declared a special cash dividend of $30 per share, worth about $13.3 billion in total
  • Payable December 4 to shareholders of record at the close of business on November 24
  • New $4 billion share repurchase program approved, running to November 2030
  • It replaces a $4 billion plan from 2023, due to expire in January 2027, under which $3.1 billion had been bought back
  • The payout is double the $15 special dividend paid in January 2024

Costco Wholesale (COST) has declared a special cash dividend of $30 per share, a one-off payout worth about $13.3 billion in total. It has also approved a new $4 billion share repurchase program, the company said in a statement on November 10.

The special dividend is payable on December 4 to shareholders of record at the close of business on November 24. It is paid on top of Costco’s regular quarterly dividend.

The new buyback authorisation runs until November 2030. It replaces a $4 billion program adopted in 2023 and due to expire in January 2027, under which the company had bought back $3.1 billion of stock. That leaves roughly $900 million of capacity unused on the old plan as it is retired.

This is the largest special dividend in Costco’s history, double the $15 per share it paid in January 2024. The retailer has made such payments every few years since 2012, usually funding them from cash on hand rather than borrowing, and shareholders had been watching for the next one.

Management had flagged the possibility. Chief Financial Officer Gary Millerchip said earlier this year that at the company’s current valuation, a special dividend is typically the most effective way to return excess cash while keeping the flexibility to invest in growth. He also noted that with the share price well above its level at the last payout, a larger cash pile would be needed to deliver a similar yield. Analysts had estimated that matching the roughly 2.4% yield of the 2024 dividend would take around $24 per share, so the $30 figure goes beyond that benchmark.

Costco’s statement did not say how the dividend or the buyback would be funded, and it included no executive commentary. The company operates 945 warehouses, 653 of them in the United States and Puerto Rico, and runs e-commerce sites in nine countries.

For shareholders, the key date is November 24, when investors must be on the register to qualify. Under standard US settlement, the shares are expected to go ex-dividend on or around that date. With this much cash going out, attention is likely to turn to how quickly Costco rebuilds its balance sheet and whether it uses the renewed buyback more actively than the last one.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: CoreWeave Q3 beats on seven key metrics, lifts full-year revenue and run-rate guidance
item.description:
A clean beat plus a guidance raise gives CoreWeave bulls the combination they look for, and it adds support to the wider AI infrastructure trade. The margin beat is the strongest signal for sentiment because it answers concerns that rapid capacity growth comes at the expense of profitability. Traders will look past the headline beat to the size of the guidance upgrade, since the raised ranges were not disclosed in the initial results. Any read-through to AI compute demand could carry over to chipmakers and data-centre names during the next US session.

---

CoreWeave beat on every line, with margins leading the way, and then raised its outlook, which puts the focus on just how large the upgrade is.

Summary:

  • Q3 revenue of around $3.7 billion, ahead of estimates near $3.6 billion
  • Loss of $1.27 per share against an expected loss of $1.46; net loss of about $710 million versus roughly $850 million expected
  • Operating income of about $207 million, more than three times the roughly $64 million forecast; adjusted operating income of around $380 million versus about $246 million
  • Adjusted EBITDA of about $2.3 billion versus around $2.05 billion expected, with a 62% margin against roughly 58% forecast
  • Full-year 2026 revenue guidance and annualised run-rate revenue guidance both raised

CoreWeave (CRWV) reported third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations on every headline measure, and the AI cloud infrastructure provider raised both its full-year 2026 revenue guidance and its annualised run-rate revenue guidance.

Revenue came in at around $3.7 billion, ahead of consensus estimates near $3.6 billion. The company posted a loss of $1.27 per share, narrower than the $1.46 loss analysts had pencilled in. Its net loss of roughly $710 million compared with expectations of about $850 million.

The bigger surprise came higher up the income statement. Operating income reached about $207 million, more than three times the roughly $64 million that analysts had forecast. On an adjusted basis, operating income was around $380 million against estimates near $246 million. Adjusted EBITDA came in at about $2.3 billion versus expectations of around $2.05 billion, and the adjusted EBITDA margin of 62% was well above the roughly 58% analysts had expected.

The gap between the operating figures and the bottom line is worth noting. CoreWeave is profitable at the operating level and generates large adjusted EBITDA, yet it still reports a net loss. In a capital-heavy business of this kind, that gap usually reflects depreciation on hardware and the cost of financing. Investors are likely to keep weighing margin strength against the cost of funding growth.

Even so, the quarter points to improving operating leverage. Beating the margin estimate by more than four percentage points suggests revenue is growing faster than the costs of delivering it. That is the central test for an infrastructure provider that is scaling up capacity.

The guidance upgrades may matter more than the beat itself. Raising both the full-year revenue outlook and the annualised run-rate forecast signals that management is confident demand for AI computing capacity will hold up through the end of the year. The headline results did not include the new guidance ranges, so the size of the upgrade compared with market expectations will be a key focus.

Investors will next look for the detail behind the raised outlook on the earnings call: the revised revenue ranges, and any comments on capacity, customer demand and capital spending plans. 

---

CoreWeave, based in New Jersey, rents out large-scale computing power built on Nvidia graphics processors to companies that train and run AI models. It started out as a crypto mining company, moved into serving AI and high-performance computing customers, and rebranded as CoreWeave in 2021. It listed on Nasdaq in March 2025, raising about $1.5 billion. Its largest contracts are with major tech and AI companies. OpenAI has committed roughly $22.4 billion, Meta about $14.2 billion through 2031, and Microsoft has historically accounted for around 70% of annual revenue. In April, Meta signed a further deal worth about $21 billion, running through 2032. Nvidia is both CoreWeave’s chip supplier and an investor in the company, and it invested another $2 billion in January 2026.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stock market close: Hot CPI leads to a selloff
item.description:
US equity futures were flat ahead of the CPI report but plunged afterwards. Fed Governor Waller set the stage for a drop when he said a reading of +0.3% on core inflation would make him consider at 50 basis point hike in December.

So when CPI was +0.3% with some caveats that could have made it higher (like a -1.2% m/m drop in used car prices) that sent a shudder through the market. US 2-year yields jump 18 bps and 10s rose above above 5%. In turn, stock markets were under pressure.

Notably, the selling was mostly contained to tech as the AI angst continues. Nvidia was down another 6% as politicians target Nvidia's chip sales to China in light of the honeypot revelation. The whole bit feels a bit scripted but that's the name of the game in Washington.  There were some decent pockets of strength and breadth was relatively balanced. Notably, there was a nice pop when it was revealed that Anthropic already has a full order book for next week's $60 billion IPO.

There was a real ebb and flow to the day but the bulls gathered themselves late for a decent close that erased much of the pain.

  • DJIA -0.3%
